An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time for $B^0_s$ mesons has been made with the help of around 37 picobarns of LHCb data from 2010. This measure allows for constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model that may influence the $B^0_s$ system and was found to be 1.440 picoseconds by employing two methods with varying degrees of uncertainty, specifically 0.096 (statistical) ± 0.008 (systematic) ± 0.003 (model-based).

This research paper focuses on the numerical solution of a stochastic control problem governed by a parabolic equation with the control variable affecting the diffusion coefficient, particularly with the presence of rough inputs; it establishes the convergence of a specific numerical discretization method and provides an alternative solution using a stochastic simulation technique known as the Monte-Carlo method.

Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of alignment in the arrivals of these particles.  Our study discovered that the distribution of the arrival directions of cosmic rays with energies exceeding 8 EeV appears to be grouped into specific patterns associated with the Milky Way, the Large Magellanic Cloud, the Small Magellanic Cloud, and the Eridanus Ring galaxy region.  We discovered that the arrival rates of cosmic rays with energies above 8 EeV that are directed towards the Galactic Center and the Galactic Anti-Center exhibit opposite periodic variations in the Earth's orbit, with periods of 1.14 years and 1.17 years respectively.  We also found that the distribution of the arrival directions of cosmic rays with energies exceeding 57 EeV that are directed towards the Earth's orbit exhibits periodic variations with a period of 1.17 years, and we detected sources of energy emissions in the arrival directions of cosmic rays with energies exceeding 8 EeV that are associated with periodic variations with the same period as the Earth's orbit, specifically in the directions of the Sco-X1 and RX J1713.7-3949.
This paper proves that every finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over any field has a specific characteristic - nilpotency.

This study provides first-time data on the fluctuations of a specific angle, known as $\Psi_n$, and magnitude, known as $v_n$, related to particle flow, which have been determined using a newly developed method for four-particle correlations. Researchers used ALICE to collect these data in high-energy Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC. Fluctuations in both angle and magnitude are evident across different centralities and become more pronounced in more central collisions and in collisions where the momentum of the particles is higher than 2 GeV/c. These findings, which have been compared to theoretical models known as iEBE-VISHNU and MUSIC, demonstrate that the patterns of these fluctuations can be replicated, but require further study to fully understand the underlying dynamics. These results also show that the magnitude of these fluctuations can be influenced by initial conditions, especially in collisions that are less central, but the source of these fluctuations in more central collisions is less clear and requires further investigation.

This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach these dependencies, with no preconditions on data quality. We establish a framework where we can efficiently determine if a set of inconsistent instances aligns with a set of dependencies, and our results demonstrate implications for data quality metrics such as data precision and estimated data cardinality. Our methods can be applied to handle instances that breach dependencies, and our case studies reveal insights into tackling inconsistencies with real-world examples, using both actual and hypothetical scenarios.

This study presents a novel dynamic econometric model called Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with external covariates, specifically designed to analyze and forecast count-based time series data. Our research demonstrates the benefits of incorporating both internal and external time-varying factors in a dynamic model, using the example of UK house prices in England. We found that a Time-Varying PAR model incorporating both a random effects component and time-varying macroeconomic variables such as the national unemployment rate, outperforms static alternatives in forecasting house price inflation. Additionally, our research highlights the superiority of the Time-Varying PAR model in forecasting house price inflation when compared to leading machine learning models.

This paper introduces Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation
that replicates key aspects of Neural Descriptor Networks (NDNs). We prove that NDFs
demonstrate SE(3)-equivariance, a critical property as it stands without proof in
the original NDN study. We leverage this property to achieve a faster and more
accurate registration process. This representation representation leads to a new
task called object alignment via a pose estimation problem, with results shown
in experiments using 3D chairs and a modified dataset of household objects.

Using the functional renormalization group at the next-to-leading order in the derivative expansion, we updated the position of $z_c/R_\chi^{1/\gamma}$ for $N=2$ O(N) universality classes from 1.609 to $2.437 \pm 0.017$, which is based on an analysis of flow equations for the quark deconfinement transition in $3d$ and includes corrections to the leading scaling assumption.

In statistics and machine learning, it is frequently essential to establish whether a basic optimization method on a non-convex function can eventually enter a region where the function becomes locally convex. To address this, we developed an inequality that enables us to analyze the properties of the optimization landscape surrounding the solutions produced by an approximate message passing (AMP) algorithm. AMP algorithms are widely used due to their efficiency and simplicity, and they often serve as the basis for various generalized approximate message passing algorithms. Our main inequality, which takes into account the properties of AMP algorithms, allows us to ensure that the non-convex function is locally convex, given certain conditions are met, with a specific rate of convergence. This achievement is particularly significant for the generalized AMP algorithms, as it guarantees that these algorithms will always converge to a local minimum, even when the input data is in its general form, rather than being randomly generated. Furthermore, our inequality-derived condition is more flexible and more easily verifiable than the existing similar results, and it can be applied to a wide range of applications and algorithms.

While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the SUPREMACY telescope at the Teacreek Observatory in Papua New Guinea, either side of an equatorial mountain range, where the same field of view shows a marked difference in brightness at different elevations. By combining data from 14 nights in 2001, we calculated the aerosol depth above 4000 meters to be 0.053 plus or minus 0.021, which matches measurements from a nearby local station with more precise instrumentation.

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has been widely adopted due to its high precision and speed. This research falls into two primary method categories: single-maximum and multi-maximum methods. In the first category, a unique regression branch is employed to predict a pose candidate from an object feature descriptor derived from a CNN. This methods' accuracy is unmatched, with a typical IoU value exceeding 60%. In the second category, multiple pose candidates are predicted by assigning a probability to each possible orientation on the horizontal axis using a special design, often referred to as the Sphere method. This research introduces a new approach called the Cylinder method, which extends the Sphere method to allow for the prediction of multiple pose candidates by assigning a probability to each possible orientation along both the horizontal and vertical axes. When applied to the SUN3D dataset, the Cylinder method achieved an accuracy of 69.2%, surpassing the current state of art. When applied to the NYUDv2 dataset, the same method achieved an accuracy of 45.5%, also surpassing the current state of art.

We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to address General Graphical Lasso
challenges. Based on the original Graphical Lasso idea by Friedman et al., who
used $l_1$ norm to achieve sparse regression and reverse engineering in Gaussian
graphical models, we have progressed significantly. Currently, Graphical Lasso
models can handle various distributions and regression methods, including both
sparse and non-sparse models. Despite its benefits, users may encounter
issues, such as the need to manually adjust hyperparameters, the difficulty of
choosing between sparse and non-sparse models, and the time consumed by the
algorithm, particularly when working with large datasets. To address these
challenges, we have developed the Graph Graphical Lasso Optimizer, a framework
combining optimization techniques and heuristic methods to enhance the
algorithm's efficiency and effectiveness. We have also integrated GGLasso with
scipy's sparse regression solvers to enhance performance, and provided a
visualizer to facilitate the interpretation of results. We have conducted
experiments to evaluate the algorithm's performance under different conditions,
and demonstrate its application in three case studies. We have open-sourced
GGLasso on GitHub, to facilitate further development and usage.

Numerous numerical methods for resolving stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics simulations have been evaluated in terms of their performance in modeling biomolecules. Recent analysis indicates that the performance of these methods in non-equilibrium simulations depends heavily on the time scale and specific algorithm used. In equilibrium simulations, the performance is largely independent of the method and is largely determined by the accuracy of the configurational averaging. The paper's key findings show that the accuracy of the averaging can be improved through the use of a sub-ensemble approach or methods that account for correlations, The paper also shows that the performance of the methods can be enhanced when using Gaussian processes in the modeling of biomolecules in their native state. The research presents novel applications of the methods in question and offers algorithms for solving stochastic differential equations with time-dependent potentials and the modeling of biomolecules with Gaussian processes. The code provided enables users to reproduce the results and adapt the methods for their own purposes.

Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks called multi-layered eigenvector centrality. In multi-layered networks, multiple connections between nodes in different layers can affect the centrality of each node. We use an operator approach and an algebraic formulation to determine the centrality of nodes within these networks. A centraliy matrix is defined based on the relationships between nodes in different layers, allowing us to calculate multi-layered eigenvector centrality through the eigenvector decomposition of this matrix. We prove that our approach produces meaningful results by ensuring they align with existing single-layer eigenvector centrality findings and provide examples demonstrating the use of multi-layered eigenvector centrality.

Recently, we generated the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra using deformed Poisson brackets, 
which effectively replicate the Fock coordinate transformation. This transformation 
corresponds to a de Sitter spacetime. In this study, we formulate the Dirac equation within 
$R$-Minkowski spacetime and establish that it is analogous to the Dirac equation defined 
within the de Sitter spacetime, described by its conformally flat metric. We then propose 
a novel strategy to solve the Dirac equation within the de Sitter spacetime by adopting 
the Schr\"{o}dinger picture.

This research examines the underlying mechanics at play when a sphere collides with a body of water, specifically the surface seal phase that occurs at the beginning of the impact. The surface seal phase, where water is displaced by the sphere's descent and air is trapped above its curved surface, was studied using high-speed imaging and a computational model. The results show that the sphere makes contact with the water's surface before being slowed by surface tension, and that the time it takes to form a sealed surface varies directly with the diameter of the sphere and inversely with the square root of the impact velocity. The same experiments were then repeated on the bottom of a pool, yielding different outcomes due to the presence of hydrostatic pressure, and the data from these experiments were used to develop an equation for the duration of the surface seal phase.

A recently introduced class of terms, effective field theory $\cal{L}_\theta$-terms or $\theta$-terms for short, have been effectively used in describing global symmetries by incorporating higher-derivative corrections. These $\theta$-terms were initially proposed as a way to explain the matter-antimatter asymmetry in the universe but were later found to be problematic due to their inability to satisfy causality in quantum field theories. Effective field theory $\theta$-terms can be made invariant under the Poincaré group, leading to their expansion into a vast array of fundamental field theories, including both quantum field theories and their extensions with higher curvature terms and various effective theories of gravity. A thorough causality analysis of these $\theta$-terms reveals that they can only be made causal within effective field theories that include a minimum of three massless vector fields and their associated higher derivative terms, effectively limiting the range of their applications.

Our calculations using first-principles methods reveal that cubanite exhibits unusual orbital selectivity, with electrons occupying certain molecular orbitals while being localized in other atomic ones. This phenomenon is exceptionally rare in 3d transition metal compounds, providing a theoretical basis for the experimentally observed lack of charge disproportionation, anomalous Mössbauer spectra, and ferromagnetic coupling between adjacent iron ions.

A burgeoning field in quantum physics, known as multi-phonon physics, is driving research and development for both fundamental understanding and applications in metrology and communication systems. Quantum acoustic resonators, which utilize the strong coupling effect between a cavity and its surrounding acoustic environment, are considered a crucial component in multi-phonon technology. While previous studies have demonstrated the coupling of microwave photons with sound waves, they lacked measurement of multiple phonon interactions. This study breaks new ground by detecting four-phonon interactions and the formation of dark excitons in III-V semiconductor quantum dots, coupled with an superconducting resonator and a quantum acoustic cavity. Due to their short lifetimes, both four-phonon interactions and the dark excitons had not been observable until now. This research utilized a theoretical model to analyze the results and revealed that the four-phonon interactions could be distinguished from loss effects, such as multi-photon decays, was possible under conditions of low temperature and quantum acoustics coupling.

Our investigation focuses on two-dimensional electronic lattices represented by a non-magnetic system made from a graphene monolayer and a layered NbSe2, which have been combined and arranged in a rectangular pattern. This system allows the manipulation of its symmetry from a square to a rectangular structure by adjusting the interlayer distance. Through theoretical calculations, we identified the Dirac cones within this electronic lattice, even at the micron scale, and determined their response to applied tension and strain. Our findings reveal that conical structures can be modified by altering the lattice dimensions, but local distortion does not significantly impact these cones due to the robustness of the graphenelike layers. However, layers with distinct orbital characteristics around the Fermi level can be separated through tension or strain, resulting in the splitting of Dirac cones along the armchair direction. Our research demonstrates that the robustness of Dirac cones in this system makes it an ideal candidate for the investigation of topological phase transitions through the controlled application of tension or strain.

Our research creates single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) via conditional processes involving single-photon fields, optical parametric amplifiers, and squeezed vacuum sources. We derive mathematical formulas for SPCCSs generated through both their bare and wrapped forms. Both theoretical and experimental/simulation data analysis are performed to evaluate key quantum characteristics of SPCCSs, including sub-poisson statistics, entanglement, and catalytic effects. Both theoretical and simulated/wrapped data demonstrate that SPCCSs can exhibit sub-poisson statistics, entanglement, and display coherent properties similar to their original counterparts. Moreover, we find that SPCCSs can be generated with $\chi^2$ distributions having large non-classical entanglement, and that they retain their entanglement for various loss levels. Additionally, we compare and contrast two methods of generating SPCCSs and find that both theories and simulations indicate that there are distinct differences based on the photon number distributions.

In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the precise solutions to Einstein's field equations. This review focuses on explaining the fundamental principles and detailed calculations of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism, specifically by converting a complex self-dual electromagnetic field from the standard Minkowski space basis to the complex null tetrad basis. As a result, we derive the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor in the context of Newman-Penrose formalism.

A recent framework combining artificial neural networks and mixed integer linear programming for designing chemical compounds has been built upon to create a new method for polymer inference. This new method incorporates a unique way of depicting polymers using monomers, new descriptors that capture their structure, and employs linear regression in the predictive framework. Computational trials have demonstrated that the proposed method is capable of accurately predicting property values for a range of parameters and can be applied to a broader set of applications, including the predictive models itself.

Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans is a challenging task due to the varying quality of these images, which can obscure the tumor and force medical professionals to rely heavily on clinical data. Deep learning techniques have made significant progress in automating tumor segmentation, but these methods often fall short for new, unseen patients with different characteristics, a problem known as "instance-specific difficulty". Our main objective was to address this difficulty by developing a method called "Multi-Instance Consistent Multi-Domain Network" (MICMDN) that can effectively use a limited set of high-quality images to train a model capable of accurately segmenting difficult esophageal tumors in new patients. In the initial stage, the model learns from easy patient data and produces a basic feature set, which it then refines to accommodate harder patients included in the training set. To ensure the model adapts to a wide range of patient types, the MICMDN uses domain-specific adaptations and ensures the model can work effectively across different patients by using a contrastive loss function. Our experiments involved using CT scans of 10 patients with difficult-to-identify tumors and 20 easier cases, and the results showed that the proposed technique significantly improved the quality of the segmentation compared to the current state of art deep learning techniques.

Multilingual individuals possess a high level of proficiency in two or more languages, enabling effective written and oral communication across multiple languages. When communicating, they may blend languages, also known as code-switching or code-mixing, by switching between different languages within a single utterance. This research explores current NLP developments, constraints, and potential obstacles in tackling five critical issues affecting multilingual communities: crisis management, healthcare, election campaigns, fake news dissemination, and hate speech. To move forward, we outline potential future datasets, models, and resources to enhance NLP applications for societal betterment, exemplified through an analysis of code-mixing between English and Hindi but with implications for other language combinations.

Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require more precise guidelines balancing visually impaired users' needs and practical description generation feasibility. High-quality reference data could be ideal for system evaluation, yet we should also consider other alternatives.

Tantalum oxide compounds, with the formula Ta$_2$O$_5$, are notable for being non-toxic and possessing a high dielectric constant, making them suitable for implantable medical devices. In search of new features, researchers studied the theoretical properties of Ta$_2$O$_5$ in its various polymorphic forms using the GGA+U method. They found that Ta$_2$O$_5$ can exist in five different structures and that the energy difference between them is very small. In order to study the dynamics of these structures under the influence of electric fields, the researchers used the frozen photon approach. They discovered that some structures exhibit nonlinear optical properties, specifically second-harmonic generation, and that the degree to which this property is displayed is directly related to the asymmetry of the structures. In addition, the researchers calculated the effective Hamiltonian that describes the dynamics of these structures and found that the Ta$_2$O$_5$ with the KTaO$_3$ structure can be well-described using a mean-field approach but that the others cannot. They also found that the dynamics of these structures can be highly nonlinear, to the point of being able to produce the third-harmonic generation signal, a property that could be useful in hadrontherapy for cancer treatment.

Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to individual factors, such as information literacy, and societal factors, such as democracy level. In contrast, our research explores how personality influences the spread of misinformation on social media. Combining two large Twitter data sets from 2014 and 2019, we collected 45 million tweets containing news-related keywords from 48 US states. We used the personality traits from the NEO Oyster project to create a model of Twitter users' personalities and applied it to the Twitter users who shared the tweets. We discovered that users high in conscientiousness were less likely to share news, including misinformation, while users high in openness were more likely to do so. We also found that the personality-driven news circulation varied significantly across states, with particularly high levels of misinformation circulation observed in states with high levels of individualism and Massachusetts.

Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of audio feedback from the instructor due to limited research focus on using speech. A crucial aspect to take into consideration is that audio guidance might be given after the demonstration is completed, as well as during the process. Our study examined how speech given after a demonstration influences a robot's ability to identify the task it should perform and how audio feedback given in real-time affects the robot's ability to execute the intended task. A feature extraction method was developed to analyze audio feedback from human instructors and distinguish between three categories: task-identifying features, action-guiding features, and warning features. The findings of the experiments suggest that the robot is capable of determining the task it should perform based on post-demonstration audio cues and that real-time audio feedback given at action-execution points can effectively be used to guide the robot's actions. A comparison between robotic learning from demonstrations that incorporate audio feedback given in real-time and those without audio revealed a significant improvement in action accuracy.

Quantum field theory complexity is particularly hard to define, especially when transitioning beyond simple free models and their corresponding Gaussian representations. A promising approach to address this difficulty is through the study of conformal field theories in 1+1 dimensions, specifically focusing on the universal sector of the energy-momentum tensor in this context. A key unifying framework consists of Euler-Arnold equations and their broader integro-differential generalizations, ensuring the well-posedness of state or operator complexity optimization problems. A recent discovery revealed that the complexity of states or operators can be determined using the geodesic equation along a specific curved metric derived from the stress-energy tensor, leading to a deeper understanding of the underlying physics. This knowledge has been successfully applied to demonstrate the non-locality inherent to complexity in systems without a clear distinction between local and non-local regions in the spacetime. A thorough examination of geodesic complexity is presented in the main body of this work, with a focus on previously established connections to the holographic principle from the theory of the AdS/CFT correspondence. Some newly derived formulations of complexity for systems without a clear separation of local and non-local regions in the spacetime are also introduced.

Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our research objectives in addressing the automation challenges faced in testing conversational systems. We began by conducting a survey among developers of active conversational systems and identified several issues with the current testing practices. Next, we presented an automated testing framework at the 2022 IJCAI workshop on Artificial General Intelligence, which was then refined based on feedback from the survey respondents and other industry experts. Our solution includes a design for testing dialog flows and a method for evaluating the trustworthiness of responses generated by language models. We also developed a prototype of the testing framework that was tested using examples, but we plan to conduct more extensive testing in the future.

Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining popularity due to the widespread use of multi-domain online services. However, most current methods are limited by either assuming non-existent domain relationships or failing to account for situations with multiple sparse domains. In reality, users often interact with multiple domains, resulting in interconnected user relationships and abundant side information available across domains. Furthermore, recommendations in such scenarios benefit from utilizing side information within each domain and identifying shared user preferences across sparse domains. In light of these challenges and opportunities, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR). This framework simultaneously handles multiple sparse domains by leveraging a global user preference matrix derived from inter-domain user connections and side information from within each domain. In doing so, it generates more precise and more domain-aware recommendations compared to traditional cross-domain methods. We conduct extensive experiments across seven real-world datasets, achieving notable improvements over the baseline methods in terms of recommendation accuracy.

Convex optimization issues often take on a more manageable form when represented with conic formulations that leverage a wide variety of exotic cones. Exotic cones in this context, refer to specialized geometric shapes with properties enabling efficient implementation of computational tools, specifically barrier oracles for their own and dual shapes. This work introduces Hypatia, an interior-point solver designed to handle these complex shapes with ease. Developed using Julia and interfacing with JuMP, Hypatia can utilize a wide assortment of predefined exotic cones. It then generates simplified equivalent formulations for various optimization applications that can provide significant improvements in processing speed and memory consumption. The proposed method demonstrates a marked improvement in problem-solving efficiency when compared to more conventional and complex conic formulations.

The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and trustworthy quality control pipelines, but effectively generalizing these methods across diverse, previously unseen data remains a significant challenge. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's ability to accurately detect artifacts on new data without retraining, utilizing large datasets from the UK Biobank and the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. A key finding reveals that models performing well on small samples may fail to generalize to larger datasets, due in part to differences in MRI protocols, demographics, and acquisition techniques used in these datasets. To improve generalization, the researchers introduced two large multi-site datasets, consisting of 30,000 and 10,000 subjects respectively, which were used to investigate factors affecting quality control across diverse data, ultimately leading to the development of enhanced preprocessing techniques, artifacts detection using deep neural networks, and a score aggregation method. These innovations resulted in a refined MRIQC pipeline, demonstrated to effectively process over 89,000 brain scans with high accuracy, achieving a 99.9% success rate in detecting severe artifacts on new, previously unseen data.

To understand how private electric vehicles influence the recovery of power grids following outages, we developed a mathematical framework that incorporates decentralized decision-making in both transportation and energy systems. We utilized multi-agent optimization to model this process and overcame computational challenges through an efficient algorithm based on precise reformation. Numerical analysis was conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, yielding valuable policy insights and paving the way for further study into grid resilience with private EVs within interconnected transportation and energy networks.

The Motivation Dynamics framework, a concept explored in recent studies that applies bifurcations to model an autonomous agent's decision-making processes, is further developed to accommodate multiple autonomous entities in this paper. We demonstrate how the framework's capabilities can be expanded to capture persistent, cooperative behavior between agents meeting at specific locations, and through in-depth analysis and numerical data, reveal that this extension exhibits a complex pattern indicative of a strange attractor.

This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, and $0.75$) using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. We studied the fundamental properties of bulk GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 materials crystallizing in the AuCu3 structure. Our results match previous experimental and theoretical data on the GdSn3 compound and indicate that CmSn3 and GdSn3 both adopt a type-A anti-ferromagnetic configuration and display metallic behavior. Notably, the magnetic moment diminishes with rising Cm content in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, and these materials share some key characteristics, rendering them promising for spintronic technology applications.

The paper reviews predictions made by an extension of the standard model called the bilepton model, which involves changing the fundamental symmetry group from $SU(2) \times U(1)$ to $SU(3)\times U(1)$, while assigning the three fermion families in a non-consecutive manner. For consistency, three fermion families are required as indicated by triangle anomaly cancellation and asymptotic freedom. In the framework of the bilepton model, novel physical particles that can be studied using existing particle accelerators include bileptons (made of two leptons), three types of heavy quarks (truth, beauty, and charm), and three types of heavy neutros (electron, muon, and tau). Theoretical calculations for cross-sections and rates of various processes are provided, along with suggestions for experimental searches at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) for these bilepton, heavy quarks and heavy neutrinos. The model also predicts unusual phenomena that can be studied using existing particle accelerators, such as deep-inelastic scattering facilities, but are now obsolete. The Bilepton model can be tested through a wide range of experiments at the LHC, both by creating these particles directly and by looking at unusual side effects on quark and lepton interactions. The paper also includes a discussion on how the bilepton model can be confirmed as a theory by observing three fermion families in the laboratory.

The concept of ordered generating sequences (OGS) extends a fundamental property of finite abelian groups to non-abelian groups, providing a distinct generalization. According to its definition, any element within a group can be expressed as a product of various generator powers, arranged in a specific order. For the symmetric group Sn, R. Shwartz established a significant link between the ordered generating sequences and the standard Coxeter presentation. Our study extends this connection to the finite classical Coxeter group Bn by standardizing the ordered generating sequences, which allows us to identify exchange laws for Bn. Additionally, we establish that the algebraic structure formed by ordered generating sequences is isomorphic to the algebraic structure formed by permutations under Coxeter operation. Our analysis also includes an in-depth examination of the geometric implications of these exchange laws for the complex reflection systems in Bn.

Utilizing the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we've developed a method to calculate weak lensing convergence by combining data on the positions and photometry of foreground galaxies. A correlation between this approach and the residual Hubble diagram values of Type Ia supernovae holds a $3.6\sigma$ significance and is consistent with dark matter effects due to galactic halos. Further investigation shows that lensing-induced changes in the observed magnitudes of Type Ia supernovae should be comparable to about 0.2 mag at $z=0.03$, although this can be accounted for by normalising the galaxy distribution based on photometry. As such, we propose an alternate explanation for the reported tension between Type Ia supernovae and baryon acoustic oscillations in the low redshift universe. Additionally, we anticipate that future large-scale distance luminosity indicators will require an understanding of weak lensing effects.

The development of reliable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on trustworthy interfaces that link light with spin. In silicon photonic technology, light interacting with point defects, specifically within the T branch of the radiation damage spectrum, could provide an ideal solution. However, research on these defect centers has been limited due to their difficult creation, and as a result, primary focus has been on researching the larger radiation damage centers with zero-chirality features. This paper reports the generation of a previously unreported amount of stimulated emission from a single silicon (110) wafer due to its unique T features, achieving a threshold power that is 7 orders of magnitude lower than previously recorded in a bulk silicon material, and 3 orders of lower than material created through implantation techniques. The unique characteristics and low threshold of this material make it an attractive starting point for developing photonic-spin interfaces based on radiation damage in silicon.

For our task that considers context, a suitable object detector is required.
This study divides object detectors taking context into account by categorizing
them based on whether they use context to aid in recognition, to define a search
space, or to provide input features.
To the best of our knowledge, there is no previous research that has organized
object detectors using context in this manner.
Our analysis of current deep learning-based object detectors reveals that
S2VD, a dataset designed to test context-aware object detection, assesses
context in three different ways, including: (1) context aiding in
recognition, (2) context defining search space, and (3) context as input
features.
Our analysis also reveals that there is no universally applicable evaluation
metric for context-aware object detection, and that different metrics are
suitable for different contexts.
Our research further explores the relationship between context and object
detection, revealing that context can take many forms and that there is no
single, representative dataset to train object detectors on.
Finally, our study highlights the challenges and potential solutions for
training object detectors that consider context, including using context as a
conditioning variable, using context to define the region of interest, and
using context to train object detectors in a multi-task setting.

The main objectives of this paper are two-fold: first, we demonstrate the existence of multiple solutions to a specific Kirchhoff type elliptic system that incorporates a concave-convex property; second, we establish an initial result for a system of this type that enables the proof of an alternative result, building upon the groundwork laid in [20, Theorem 1.1, Theorem 1.2].

This paper introduces a matrix-valued version of the strong Rayleigh property and related bounds in the complex case. We show that the VTE (Vector Tile Ensemble) criterion is more restrictive than the SRC (Strongly Representative Covariance) condition in both real and complex settings. The real case builds on previous research, while new results in the complex case include a non-uniform grid-based derivation of the SRC condition and subsequent inequalities based on the strong Rayleigh property. These inequalities provide expected lower bounds on the test error when considering the variance of a parametric model or sampling bias. The complex setting can be applied to data with non-independent and potentially non-stationary entries in the feature space.

Wilberd van der Kallen translated this 1951 thesis into English, originally written by T.A. Springer. Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K), specifically focusing on fields K with a characteristic other than two. His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant characteristics. These characteristics initially mirror those found in the general linear group – namely, irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers – but also incorporate additional properties, such as unique configurations of Hermitian forms and quadratic forms, each belonging to a specific equivalence class.

A key challenge in kidney transplants arises from the incompatibility between donors and patients, which has been exacerbated by the growing scarcity of kidney donors. Desensitization techniques aim to make transplants possible between incompatible pairs by significantly reducing the immune system's reaction. These methods are costly, time-consuming, and may pose additional health risks for patients. Patients receiving incompatible transplants may face higher rates of transplant rejection, infections, and other complications, and are more likely to lose their transplants. A promising approach to address this issue involves using kidney transplants with incompatible donors from the same ethnic group, assuming that genetic similarities could minimize incompatibility. A study published in the journal Nature Medicine found that patients from the same ethnic group who are incompatible over the Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) system may be suitable candidates for kidney transplants with low rejection rates, especially if the incompatibility is limited to four or fewer HLA loci. Furthermore, the study indicates that the risk of transplant rejection decreases as the time elapsed since the transplant increases, and that patients with incompatible matches at the A, B, C, and D HLA loci but compatible matches at the E HLA locus may also be good candidates.

This paper explores the relationship between word2vec representations and the co-occurrence matrix representing the patterns of word co-occurrence within a given text corpus. We highlight that the information contained in word2vec models, specifically whether a word can be recognized, is independent of the distribution of the words themselves and instead depends on the pairwise relationships with other words. We then examine the theoretical framework in which these models can be learned, showing under mild conditions that learning the word2vec model is possible even when only training data consists of local samples drawn from the co-occurrence patterns defined by a parametric model. We then discuss three experiments using a model that generates co-occurrence patterns, a word2vec adversarial training model, and real-world data sets. We conclude by discussing potential applications and future research in this area.

This article presents the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based IDET systems as alternatives to our previously proposed optimal wideband waveforming strategy in [1].
Fair-throughput and sum-throughput optimisation problems are defined and formulated.
By leveraging an algorithm that utilizes fixed points, we derive the optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput values for SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems.

This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we've developed a numerical strategy utilizing Cartesian grids to efficiently handle complex boundary transformations and high-resolution interface representation. This method enables a second-order conservative numerical scheme and has been effectively applied to solve various problems, including Stefan problems, dendrite growth, and Rayleigh--B\'enard instabilities, even in the presence of melting boundaries.

In multiagent learning settings with general strategy spaces, we establish the first proofs that after a finite number of steps, learned policies will reach a Coarse Correlated Equilibrium (CCE) via two different algorithms. Firstly, we show that using a simple exploration-exploitation algorithm in a multiagent learning environment will lead to a CCE in a finite number of steps. Secondly, we prove that agents using a more advanced algorithm called Linear Individual Q-learning will also reach a CCE within a finite number of steps. It's essential to note that achieving a Correlated Equilibrium (CE) is unattainable through these algorithms due to the complexity of the underlying game, as demonstrated by a counterexample.

An analysis of a stochastic Susceptible to Infective to Recovered model is conducted, where the model is based on an Erdős-Rényi random graph that changes dynamically as susceptible individuals connected to infected neighbours form new connections or sever existing ones. As the model is scaled to accommodate large populations, researchers obtained mathematical proofs of key properties of the model, particularly its early stages and the phase where the epidemic spreads rapidly. They also found that under certain conditions, there are sharp thresholds where the model suddenly switches between two completely different behaviours. It has been proven that these transitions are more dramatic if the model is changed to only form new connections to uninfected individuals, where the model suddenly switches from no infections to complete spread.

Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of these components is straightforward for simple objects like scalar functions, it presents a challenge for complex quantities like cross sections due to differences in notation, units, and collinear dependencies. This issue is particularly pronounced when fitting PDFs, as even a seemingly minor discrepancy among input data can lead to significantly different estimates of fit parameters. To address this problem, we've developed an integrated toolkit that automates the process of normalizing input predictions, ensuring they conform to standard notation, units, and scaling, which can be applied in PDF fitting applications.

To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple influencing factors, reinforcement learning agents can effectively utilize previously collected historical data. Standard experience replay enables agents to retain information from prior iterations. However, the current approach equally values all collected observations, neglecting their varying significance. A more adaptive method, the variance reduction based experience replay framework, selectively leverages the most informative historical data. This approach prioritizes past observations more likely to represent the current target distribution. Theoretical and practical evaluations demonstrate that this method accelerates optimal policy discovery and boosts the effectiveness of state-of-the-art policy optimization methods.

In our examination of a single person engaging in multiple conversations with 
different partners, we discovered a significant shortfall in available datasets. 
Our newly created resource, the MultiTalk Dataset, aims to address this issue, 
featuring 32 extensive dialogues (around 7,500 words) between a single speaker 
and four distinct conversation partners at different points in time. This dataset 
has four key characteristics: extended dialogues, varying timeframes, different 
partners, and spoken language. It demonstrates promise in evaluating and fine-
tuning models for multi-talk settings and has the potential to contribute to 
related research areas. Our code and dataset are available online at the addresses 
listed below.

We introduce MG-GLAM, a computational tool developed to rapidly create
N-body simulations for a broad category of modified gravity models. These
models, including f(R)-gravity and $n$-einstein theories, are designed to
improve the FGLM algorithm used for calculating the gravitational potential
and metric modifications in these theories. Using these calculations, we
created N-body simulations that can be used to predict the behavior of these
modified gravity models in the cosmos. Our code has several key advantages,
including the ability to produce simulations at rates that are 10-100 times
faster than existing methods, due in large part to our use of an N-body
distribution that remains unchanged throughout the simulation. This allows
us to bypass time-consuming methods of solving the nonlinear equations
describing the evolution of the cosmos, instead solving the linear equations
that describe the relationship between the gravitational potential and the
distribution of matter. We also developed an algorithm to calculate the
metrical forces that drive the evolution of the cosmos in these modified
gravity models, using a pseudo-N-body method that we tested and validated
against the original N-body simulations. Our simulations can be used to
create mock galaxy catalogues that have been observed in real galaxy surveys.

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes on the complex plane, specifically exploring connections to the Dyson model and the SLE$_\kappa(\rho)$ process for $\kappa>0$ and $\rho>0$. One notable result establishes that the Dyson model and the SLE$_\kappa(\rho)$ process can drive Gaussian free field-valued processes in the plane under the Schramm flow and the heat flow, respectively. Additionally, this paper demonstrates that the weak convergence of the Dyson model and the SLE$_\kappa(\rho)$ process is reflected in the associated Gaussian free field-valued processes under the weak topology. Furthermore, it shows that these processes have the property of local absolute continuity, given one is absolutely continuous to another, a result that generalizes a previous finding by the authors.

MediaWiki's 'WorkingWiki' is an open-source extension that converts
a wiki into a sophisticated collaborative platform for writing
software projects, expressed in languages like C, Java, and Python.
It integrates multiple features to facilitate seamless coding and
project development, utilizing the power of the wiki's built-in
features such as discussion pages, macros, and templating engines.
Code is written directly into the wiki pages using embedded
languages, and the 'include' function allows for easy management
of project files, minimizing the need for external file management.
The 'WorkingWiki' extension also features an advanced code highlighting
and formatting system, along with the ability to execute code
snippets and track changes made to the codebase. The source code
for the extension is available on GitHub, providing developers with
freedom to modify and customize it according to their needs.

This research investigated the underlying causes of a complex phenomenon known as "negative d'Alembert paradox" that occurs during flame studies, especially in regards to heat release fluctuations affecting acoustic flame driving forces. The study employed a multi-zone model that accounted for the movement of gas flows and heat release within the flame, in addition to a linearized model of a flame scanning technique known as Laser-Induced Fluorescence (LIF). The study compared three models of a flame: one static model, one model with heat release fluctuations, and one model that took into account the movement of gas flows. The results showed that the static model failed to accurately predict the oscillation frequencies found in the Rijke tube, while the model with heat release fluctuations was able to predict these frequencies accurately. The study also found that the model that accounted for the movement of gas flows made minimal improvements to predicting flame driving forces. The study concluded that heat release fluctuations are the primary cause of negative d'Alembert paradox, and that the movement of gas flows has a negligible effect on these fluctuations.

We investigate the neutrinoless double beta decay driven by an extremely light dark matter field interacting with neutrinos, particularly focusing on the impact when this interaction breaches the lepton number, which directly leads to a significant influence on the $0
u  eta  eta$ decay, even when neutrino masses are very small. Since the ultralight dark matter can be adequately modeled as a classical field, this interaction's effects are evident in a semi-analytical form, revealing that the $0 
u  eta  eta$ decay rate must exceed the dark matter density by several orders of magnitude. Furthermore, considering that the dark matter density is approximately $0.003$ geometric mass units per cubic kilometer, we find that a future experiment capable of detecting $0 
u  eta  eta$ decay decay rates exceeding $10^{-2}$ per second would be able to set a lower limit on the mass of this type of dark matter at approximately 10 microeV, provided that the current $0 
u  eta  eta$ decay lifetime limit holds.

Nonlocal gravity theory is a classical generalization of Einstein's gravity theory. Based on an analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics, this new model involves a history-dependent relation that can be confirmed through data. The purpose of this paper is to modify nonlocal gravity theory so that the nonlocal aspect relates directly to observable properties, similar to the approach in nonlocal electrodynamics. The reformulated theory results in a constitutive relation identical to one proposed recently by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl. The nonlocal gravity theory can be applied to show that de Sitter spacetime does not meet the theory's requirements.

Understanding how genomic elements affect specific traits through genome-wide association studies remains complex due to the sheer number of available annotations. We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint relevant genomic elements, based on associations across the entire genome, by identifying patterns of influence in trait-associated SNPs. This approach can incorporate multiple annotation types and has been successfully applied to 13 human traits such as blood cell types, metabolic disorders, and inflammatory diseases, using data from a comprehensive resource covering 46 genomic features. Our approach has been improved to accommodate recent large-scale genomic resources and have found that features influencing traits often do so in a localized manner, within 50 kilobases. Furthermore, we've observed that certain annotation types, such as DNase-I hypersensitive sites, influence traits in a widespread manner, often affecting 1-10 megabases of surrounding DNA, and accounting for a significant proportion of associated SNPs, up to 70%. We've made available an interactive web tool, called AnnoGA, for researchers to explore and incorporate genomic elements into their analyses and analyses pipelines.

This paper discusses recent findings from the LHC involving small systems studied
by the ALICE, ATLAS and CMS collaborations. Due to the growing significance
of QCD in small systems, particularly in situations with high multiplicity, the
attempts to identify collective behavior in these systems are crucial. The current
research demonstrates that quark gluon plasma formation is not exclusive to large
collision systems and that characteristics of heavy flavor quarks in intermediate
systems require further study. The potential of the LHC for future research
includes the study of intermediate systems involving protons and ions, the use
of unique detectors like the ALICE and CMS multiplicity systems, and the potential
for future collisions at the LHC and future colliders like the HL-LHC and lepto-electron
colliders. The future research will enable a deeper understanding of hadron
nucleus and nucleus nucleus interactions, the production of heavy flavor quarks in
intermediate systems, and the formation of quark gluon plasma in small systems.

Observations of X-ray variability in the cosmos have uncovered a class of sources called low-mass X-ray binaries that contain compact objects called neutron stars. By monitoring these sources for changes in X-ray output, researchers have obtained extensive data sets that researchers have used to test fundamental theories about the behavior of matter under extreme pressures and temperatures. However, analyzing these data sets has been hampered by a lack of effective algorithms, particularly for detecting repeating patterns. Another notable issue is that the locations and starting points of time series data sets are often uncertain or missing. To address these limitations, a method is proposed to analyze time series data sets that contain locations and starting points, incorporating a non-negative matrix factorization technique to enhance the quality of the data and a Gaussian process to model the repeating patterns. The performance of the algorithm is tested on simulated data sets and real data sets of a low-mass X-ray binary called GRS 1757-425, which contains a neutron star. The analysis provides a better understanding of the source's variability and helps identify any changes that may have occurred over time, in addition to facilitating the creation of high-quality data sets that can be used to test the behavior of matter at extreme pressures and temperatures.

THz radiation enables the precise stimulation of vibrational frequencies in molecules and crystals, leading to the introduction of inertial influences on electrons. By drawing a comparison to classical mechanics, where circular motion generates Coriolis and centrifugal forces, analogous effects arise, specifically spin-rotation coupling, centrifugal field coupling, and the interplay of these forces with the spin-orbit and the redshift of energy levels. This distinction highlights the unique characteristics of a nonequilibrium situation, distinct from the nonequilibrium spin-orbit interaction observed in molecules under high-intensity laser fields. The unique characteristics of these inertial electron dynamics make them responsive to the spatial and temporal patterns of THz radiation, allowing for the controlled manipulation of energy levels and the creation of nonequilibrium chemical bonds within molecules and crystals.

Improving neural conversational agents' ability to produce diverse, engaging responses in casual conversations is a challenge. To tackle this issue, this paper introduces two significant innovations. Firstly, it proposes a new assessment metric called Natural Language Inference (NLI) diversity, which gauges the variety of responses generated by assessing their semantic relationships with the input query. NLI diversity assesses the degree to which each response is a logical consequence or contraindication of the initial prompt. Secondly, this paper also introduces a novel strategy for enhancing response diversity, grounded in the concept that responses can be ranked along a continuum from highly relevant to less relevant to the prompt. Based on this insight, a new diversity-boosting model is proposed, which employs a simple ranking system to differentiate responses and generate new ones from the more diverse end of the spectrum. Experiments conducted on two conversational datasets demonstrate that NLI diversity improves upon existing metrics and that the proposed approach outperforms baseline models in post-processing evaluation experiments.

The occurrence of sustainable hydrogen burning in very low-mass stars might be impacted by rotation due to the addition of centrifugal force and potential break-up caused by rapid spinning. Computer simulations model rotating low-mass stars with the capability for sustained nuclear reactions, considering a range of rotation rates, rather than slow rotation alone. Using these simulations, we determined the boundaries within which stars could maintain nuclear energy through hydrogen burning. These boundaries varied based on angular momentum. However, above a certain threshold (approximately 8.85 x 10^48 erg s) the boundaries broke into two distinct branches, resulting from objects losing mass and experiencing extreme spin. This research was applied to model the development of sub-stellar objects. Two possible scenarios were modeled: one with external forces gradually slowing the star, mainly controlled by spin-down time, and another where the star spins out of control, ultimately shedding mass and shrinking.

The technique of amplitude analysis in hadron decay studies is quite effective, 
However, this analysis faces a major challenge in addressing instrumental influences 
such as fluctuations in background and selection efficiency across different kinematic 
regions. This article will review traditional methods and current practices in 
solutions, as well as emerging approaches and potential developments in this field. 
Strategies discussed here include common techniques currently employed and 
potential future developments, with an emphasis on mathematical and statistical 
aspects.

A new model based on a comprehensive expression for radiation energy has been proposed, and it effectively elucidates the dynamics of afterglows in multiple contexts, including relativistic, non-relativistic phases and fireball radiations with radiative and adiabatic components.

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet may be accomplished through local repositioning of nodes. We have developed an algorithmic approach, alongside a theoretical proof, demonstrating that edge crossings can be minimized to zero in a broad category of edge-orderings, based on a simple sorting criterion. This algorithm's time complexity is capped at $O(n^7)$, where n denotes the number of nodes within the graph. We have tested this algorithm against existing optimization techniques for bipartite graphs, showcasing improved performance in a wide range of scenarios, including a significant reduction in crossings for a real-life data set consisting of 102 nodes.

This research focuses on a bipedal robot that uses both legs and thrusters to move on the ground, specifically on a solid planetary surface with an atmosphere. A key aspect of this robot is its ability to use walking legs in conjunction with small propellers to create lift and increase mobility. A finite state automaton-based controller is developed to ensure the robot's stability and prevent it from falling over. A simulation model is created to test various environments and scenarios, including different surface pressures, atmospheric conditions, and terrain obstacles. The results show that this robot can move around and adjust its height to clear overlying terrain features, indicating its potential for exploring difficult planetary terrain.

Becker-Denef-Lipschitz first observed in 1979 that over finite fields $k$, the total residue map $\text{res}$ from Laurent series to $k$ is expressible in a specific language, provided $t$ is included as a parameter. This discovery motivated further research into the properties of a specific mathematical theory related to valued fields. In the course of these investigations, the authors proved that this theory does not have a certain desirable feature and demonstrated that, for infinite fields $k$, the associated power series fields cannot be computationally decided. This, in turn, led to an analogous undecidability conclusion for a specific complex-valued field of power series.

In order to enhance side-channel attacks, this research introduces a new technique called Performance Degradation through Loop Manipulation (PDL). PDL takes advantage of the loop instruction capabilities found in recent CPU architectures, specifically SMT designs. Following the introduction of PDL, the technique is applied to improve a timing attack called the Spectre Jit-based Attack. The research demonstrates how PDL can be utilized on real hardware and virtual machines to carry out enhanced side-channel attacks. The results indicate that employing PDL on top of existing micro-optimization techniques is capable of significantly enhancing the performance of side-channel attacks, with the PDL-enhanced attack exhibiting a 100-fold increase in data disclosure efficiency compared to the baseline attack on a recent SMT hardware platform. The research also explores various PDL implementation strategies and identifies areas for the improvement of future work.

A knot in an embedded $3$-dimensional submanifold of a $4$-dimensional oriented manifold is considered an interestingsubobject of the pair consisting of the manifold and the knot itself. Unknotting operations provide a way to transform this knot into a circle through a series of Reidemeister moves, facilitated by local moves that can be performed within a tubular neighborhood of the knot. A non-abelian universal property of these operations yields a natural correspondence between them and the generators of the knot's braid monoid. Consequently, a knot can be classified based on its unknotting properties, effectively redefining it as a object in the category of surfaces equipped with knots as morphisms. This framework ultimately gives rise to a new, more intricate structure known as the spin structure on these surfaces.

We develop an approach to calculating Vassiliev invariants of link classes in the $n$-dimensional space, based on the properties of maps from a simplicial complex to the space. This method allows us to create invariants of specific order, using a systematic method to barian a subset of these invariants. Our technique includes the development of a method to barian the set of invariants associated with a simplicial map, by removing or combining a subset of invariants defined by a specific pattern. We apply this method to calculate a set of 2-dimensional Vassiliev invariants for the figure-eight knot, and determine their braid-like invariants corresponding to the standard braid representing the figure-eight knot.

In cooperative systems with multiple agents, coordination enables tasks to be performed that would be beyond the capabilities of any single agent. We investigate the concept of coordination through strategic decision-making, focusing on a scenario where agents select between two tasks of varying difficulty that are randomly distributed and partially known. It has been found that a stable state of cooperation, characterized by a straightforward linear pattern, can be achieved when there is a wide range of possible action sizes. Furthermore, it was discovered that actions that maximize cooperation can be found using a simple linear optimization process that takes into account the mean and standard deviation of the random variable representing the difficulty of the environment. A computational example is used to demonstrate the applicability of these findings.
