A distinctive feature of neural development is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei
between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue as interkinetic nuclear
migration (IKNM) unfolds. In this process, new neurons are born in the upper layer and
their nuclei move downward, while dying cell nuclei move upward to the surface. We
observed that the migration pattern associated with IKNM creates a circular flow of cell
nuclei, which we believe is influenced by a vortex dynamics model. Using open-source
software, we simulated a simple model of IKNM and found that it mimics the observed
spatiotemporal distribution of cell nuclei. Furthermore, we calculated the fractal
dimension of the neuroepithelial layer during IKNM and found that it remains constant
across different stages of development. We also explored the effects of varying model
parameters on the neuroepithelial layer's fractal dimension.

In various image processing tasks, including video compressed sensing and color image demosaicing, images must be separated from coded measurements that represent their superposition. Real-world code patterns, which are often non-negative, systematically structured and non-Gaussian, can impede reconstruction performance due to their non-ideal coherence properties. This research addresses this challenge by developing optimized non-negative sparse encoding methods that prioritize code patterns' simplicity over accuracy, resulting in coded measurements that can be accurately reconstructed using popular compressed sensing methods with non-sparse solutions. A separate section of results showcases the successful application of these methods to video compressed sensing and color image demosaicing.

We've developed a comprehensive hydrodynamic theory that applies to polar active fluids in the presence of randomly distributed inclusions, and our model demonstrates the possibility of overcoming these obstructions to maintain a non-zero overall speed. Contrary to previous assumptions, the dynamics of this specific class of active matter cannot be accurately captured using simplified hydrodynamic models when the spatial environment is two-dimensional up to five-dimensional space; however, we were able to derive precise, dimension-dependent scaling parameters for these dimensions.

The growth of Information Technology has significantly altered how information is shared, making it necessary to convert printed documents into digital formats.  There has been a rise in fraudulent activities lately.  To prevent these types of fraud, it is essential to extract information from ID documents such as driving licenses and passports.  Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology can convert scanned images of these documents into readable text.  However, the accuracy of the results depends on the technique used to capture the images.  To address this challenge, an algorithm was developed to capture high-quality images of ID documents from low-quality mobile camera photos.  The first step in capturing these images involves using a mobile application to take a photo of the document, followed by capturing multiple photos from different angles.  The algorithm then selects the best image from these captures.  To ensure the accuracy of the results, the algorithm was tested on 300 different images, achieving an accuracy rate of 84.33%.  To improve the accuracy further, the algorithm was trained on 5000 different images, achieving a accuracy rate of 93.33%.  To evaluate the algorithm, a mobile application was developed to capture the images and test the algorithm in real-time scenarios.

Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either steady-state driving forces varying in intensity or driving forces that changed over time. Calculations of position expectations were carried out for multiple scenarios of mass, angular frequency, and the lambda parameter in both cases. Constant driving led to coherent states, with theoretical predictions closely matched by both simulation approaches. A discrete-time lattice Metropolis algorithm was used to evaluate the imaginary time path integral for these simulations.

The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids due to its substantial influence on their net torque. As a result, this effect must be considered when studying and modeling the evolution of their rotation patterns. We propose an analytical model to calculate the YORP acceleration for triaxial asteroids with arbitrary rotation periods and temperatures. This model is based on the application of rotational averaging methods and considers the Yarkovsky and photothermal effects simultaneously. By comparing our model with a previously established model assuming a non-rotating asteroid, we found that the difference in YORP accelerations is relatively small, especially at longer rotation period scales. However, for temperatures above 10 K, the current model yields a non-zero YORP acceleration due to the rotation-induced temperature gradient, which can lead to a significant increase in the YORP acceleration. This acceleration enhancement can result in a short rotation period scale (around a few million years) and may lead to spin-up and 180-degree flips in asteroids with initial rotation periods between 3-6 hours for surface types with high albedo. We also developed a simple numerical integrator to solve the orbital evolution equations, taking into account the YORP acceleration and radiation torques from solar gravity. By integrating these effects over time, we found that close approaches with other asteroids or planetary bodies can cause temporary increases in rotation velocity, potentially resulting in spin-up and 180-degree flips

We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action on the surface has non-negative entropy, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure.

Multiple formal models can equivalently define functions through input-output relationships, and in many cases, a natural pairing exists between these models and topological properties. In the context of automata theory, the relationship between computability and topological continuity has been extensively explored for various models, including Turing machines and finite state machines. However, a long-standing open question has arisen, particularly concerning continuous functions that map from the reals to the reals, with regards to whether the ability to compute them automatically implies they are continuous. This issue is addressed by creating a method to generate a wide range of recognizable languages through the use of continuous functions that map from the reals to the reals, effectively providing an alternate definition of such functions in relation to recognizable languages. As a result, it is demonstrated that the ability to compute these functions is equivalent to their automatic continuity, and this is achieved without relying on the ability to compute the partial functions defined by these functions on the set of real numbers.

A new type of reservoir computing, taking place in the future, builds on past concepts and improves training data efficiency and forecasting accuracy, surpassing previous records. This advanced model, incorporating a complex neural network architecture, is demonstrated in a real-world application, where a pseudorandom generator using a neural network predicts an optical fiber's noise patterns and their subsequent impacts on a phase-sensitive amplifier. Through simulation, this reservoir, capable of handling non-linear processes, can reduce training data needed for forecasting over tenfold while boosting forecasting accuracy tenfold. This cutting-edge approach, implemented using a delayed neural network with four units, successfully replicates the behavior of this specific device, sensitive to noise over several milliseconds, using minimal training, and accurately predicts the phenomena that damage it, ending with a potential application in generating anti-jitters used in optical true-random number generators.

To address scalability issues with Eulerian methods for finding optimal controllers under constraints and worst-case disturbances in variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs formulations, we've developed a second-order successive sweep algorithm for calculating the reachable state space. This approach, which assumes a continuous and smooth Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, enables us to determine the states that can be reached within a given time frame under worst-case conditions and state feedback control.

The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, suggesting that animacy exists along a spectrum rather than a binary divide. Recent evidence indicates two possible explanations for this continuum: one based on cognitive properties and another rooted in neural response patterns to action cues. The present study aims to further explore these hypotheses through the examination of TLP-induced changes in the VTC's animacy representation. Our previous findings revealed that the introduction of action words broadens the VTC's animacy representation, with the current study expanding on this by comparing the effects of action words to those of actual observed actions on the same participants. Our results show that observed actions have a more pronounced effect on the VTC's animacy representation compared to action words, leading to a more unified representation of humans and animal agents in response to observed actions. On the other hand, action words are found to induce a more distinct separation between humans and animal agents. Our study contributes to the ongoing debate surrounding the VTC's animacy spectrum by highlighting the significant impact of action perception and production on the underlying cognitive mechanisms.

The study proves the nonexistence of Landau-Siegel zeros or confirms quantum unique ergodicity for GL_2 Hecke-Maass newforms at a calculable pace, supported by the broader conclusion that Dirichlet L-function zeros exert a force pushing zeros from all other automorphic L-functions off the s=1 axis.

We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare logic originally proposed in (Unruh, POPL 2019) to incorporate "expectations" into preconditions and postconditions, thereby enabling the quantification of pre-/postconditions that reflect the relationship between programs' inputs and outputs when comparing pairs of programs.

The rapid transmission and severe impact of certain infectious diseases, such as COVID-19, highlight the critical influence of super-spreader events that significantly increase the effective basic reproduction number $R_0$. We developed a general model incorporating super-spreader events to better understand their effects on $R_0$ and the resulting epidemic outcomes. We applied this model to analyze the 2020 COVID-19 outbreak in Wuhan, China, incorporating data from various sources, including travel records and super-spreader events. Our analysis revealed that the effective $R_0$ in Wuhan exceeded 10 in late January 2020, primarily due to super-spreader events rather than general community transmission. We further simulated different epidemic scenarios based on historical data and found that the intense early outbreak in Wuhan was largely driven by super-spreader events, whereas in other cities it was more likely caused by widespread community transmission. We also compared and contrasted our model with other existing models, highlighting the significant impact of assuming non-homogeneous transmission rates, especially in calculating $R_0$.

Let's consider a complex topological vector space, denoted as X, along with the collection L(X) of continuous linear operators that act on X. This paper and its companion establish two significant categories of codiskcyclicity for operators within L(X), codiskcyclicity of the first kind and codiskcyclicity of the second kind. We prove that an operator is codiskcyclic of the second kind if it has a nontrivial invariant subspace that is topologically one-dimensional. Additionally, we demonstrate that codiskcyclicity of the first kind and codiskcyclicity of the second kind are equivalent for operators acting on infinite-dimensional one-sided Banach spaces.

The paper addresses the problem of bias in vector magnetic field maps, particularly in estimating the component perpendicular to the line-of-sight, B_perp. It was found that this bias is significant, especially near polar regions and at low altitudes above the photosphere. The study identified two primary sources of this B_perp bias: (1) image inversion methods, where CHAOS inversions exhibited notable bias, especially near the poles, and (2) data inputs, particularly with noisy and inaccurate magnetograms. Furthermore, the research revealed that the magnitude of the perp component bias gamma is directly related to the availability of longitudinal information, magnetogram noise, and the presence of polar circular features. It was also shown that combining local correlation flight inversions and current-free potential extrapolations could mitigate the bias, but the gamma value would still depend on the distribution of magnetic flux. It was further found that the bias extends to higher altitudes above the photosphere and that the magnitude of gamma varies non-linearly with the contribution of chromospheric and photospheric data. It was also observed that the bias affects the calculation of quantities derived from the magnetic field, such as the total magnetic flux, area of polar regions, flux transport parameter alpha, and the rate of flux emergence beta. It was recommended that future research should focus on developing inversion methods that minimize the perp component bias and consider adding flux conservation to the list of assumptions. It was also proposed that the perp component bias be accounted for

A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem.

Given any non-erasing free monoid morphism σ and subshift X, we define their complexity functions P_X and P_{σ(X)} in relation to free monoids N^k, where N represents the set of natural numbers, and establish that P_{σ(X)} precedes P_X in the subshift ordering. Additionally, P_{σ(X)} and P_X share a common growth rate, leading to the conclusion that the ensemble of subshifts that result from applying σ to X are characterized as those whose growth rates are greater than 2∛3 times P_X, to a sublinear factor.

By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-augmentation method known as ReCross, which employs unlabeled samples to selectively draw from existing data, fine-tune the model for better performance.
The proposed method seamlessly integrates both high-quality labeled data and the enhanced model for improved outcomes.
Our approach was tested on nine tasks from the MultiTask Dialogue Dataset, and the results showed that ReCross surpasses non-zero-shot baselines and compares favorably to unsupervised few-shot methods.

Optimizing hyperparameters in the private version of the stochastic gradient descent algorithm is a critical issue due to limited access to private datasets for hyperparameter tuning. The development of algorithms that efficiently find optimal hyperparameters for a favorable balance between privacy and performance within a predetermined search space is, therefore, crucial. In this paper, a generalized framework is established to determine an optimal balance between privacy and performance, and three cost-effective algorithms are systematically examined within this framework: evolutionary optimization, Bayesian methods, and reinforcement learning. The results of our experiments, conducted using MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning, show significant improvements over the conventional grid search method. The paper addresses existing challenges and potential research directions in the field, including solutions to enhance the transfer learning ability, leverage multiple models, and employ more efficient algorithms. The code for this research is available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/zhongyong-wang/private-hyperparameter-tuning.

For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring Ragnarsson and Tenner's previous work. By applying discrete Morse theory, we identify the homotopy type of these boolean complexes for a significant subset of Coxeter groups, including finite groups, revealing that their homotopy type is equivalent to that of a collection of spheres with dimension |S|-1. Moreover, we derive straightforward, recursive formulas to compute the number of spheres within this collection.

A comprehensive analysis of elemental abundances in low-metallicity stars within the Leo A dwarf spheroidal galaxy has been completed, using a combination of spectroscopic and photometric data from two space telescopes. A unique approach was employed to model the abundances of 24 elements for 22 stars, accounting for the effects of supernovae and stellar evolution. The analysis revealed a 'prompt' component associated with Type II supernovae and a 'delayed' component linked to Type Ia supernovae and neutron star mergers, with the latter becoming more significant at lower metallicities. The model revealed a large range of metallicity within the galaxy, with a central region exhibiting a gradient of increasing metallicity towards the center. The findings support previous observations of a dichotomy in star formation histories, with the galaxy exhibiting a complex and dynamic history. The analysis also provided a precise determination of the local chemical environment, allowing for a better understanding of the galaxy's local chemical context.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences due to delayed response resulting from the prevalence of health crisis-related online rumors, especially in China. This study aims to develop an individual-level and collective-level spread model for online rumors by utilizing the theory of diffusion. It then proposes a novel rumor-spreading indicator (RSI) to track and analyze the spread of online rumors. This study further conducts a survey among netizens in China to gather first-hand data about factors contributing to the spread of online rumors, including their credibility, fear factor, and social connectivity. The collected data are utilized to assess the constructed variables in the rumor-spreading model through survey responses from 2012 participants in China. The results reveal that factors such as the perceived truthfulness of the information, fear induced by the pandemic, social connections, and media channels through which the information was encountered significantly influence the spread of online rumors. The RSI indicator can effectively capture the rapid spread of online rumors in the early stages and slow down in the latter stages. This research contributes to the development of an individual-level and collective-level model for the spread of online rumors and provides policy-makers with valuable insights to combat the dissemination of health crisis-related online rumors.

A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been discovered by examining extragalactic planetary nebulae, specifically due to their nearly universal brightness pattern. Determining the precise distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae analysis relies on identifying and analyzing these nebulae, and a study has been conducted to discover and characterize such objects in the nearby spiral galaxy, Leo I. Using data from the Advanced Camera for Surveys (ACS) on board the Hubble Space Telescope, a comprehensive catalog of planetary nebulae candidates was created, comprising 237 objects on the galaxy's central bulge and the outer regions. A sophisticated statistical method was then used to remove false positives, resulting in 137 confirmed planetary nebulae located within the central region, the bulge, and the halo. By comparing observed magnitudes of the detected PNe and applying their intrinsic brightness values, the study was able to create a model showing the distribution of stars that formed PNe in the past 25 million years. This information was then used to calculate the total luminosity of the current stellar population in Leo I, and the study found it to be 10.1 times the current value, placing Leo I among the dwarf spheroidal galaxies with the most massive central bulges. Additionally, the study derived a stellar mass loss rate in the halo, roughly 10 times higher than previously recorded, and provided a comprehensive catalog of PNe standard candles useful for measuring the distances to similar nearby galaxies.

Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of physiological data from their patients, leading to an escalating interest in conducting statistical analyses for these rich datasets, worth millions of dollars in clinical value. Presently, researchers face significant challenges in processing this vital medical information due to the lack of suitable big data processing tools that can handle high-speed, real-time streams of physiological data with high precision. To address this limitation, we introduce LifeStream, a pioneering engine designed to process high-speed streams of physiological data at scale, surpassing the performance of leading stream processing engines like Flink by an order of magnitude while providing robust support for complex statistical analyses typical in medical research. To achieve optimal results, LifeStream leverages sophisticated techniques, incorporating multi-dimensional array optimizations, sophisticated memory management, and intelligent scheduling, and our experiments across multiple datasets and use cases demonstrate LifeStream's remarkable speed, accuracy, and durability.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in two-dimensional Euclidean space. A new category, called the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve, is defined to fill this gap and its characteristics are identified for curves in a four-dimensional Euclidean space.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, our objective is to investigate how loss function impacts performance in a simple classification context using convolutional neural networks. Our findings reveal that certain loss functions performing well in unsupervised settings when data is abundant do not generalize to scenarios with limited data, whereas some risk minimization methods, especially the robust optimization approach, are more resilient in such situations. Our results demonstrate a significant performance improvement when using the SVM loss function, which is derived from robust optimization, in classification tasks involving small datasets.

This research aims to advance the understanding of thermomechanical behavior in polymer crystallization. Strain-induced crystallization plays a significant role in polymer mechanical and thermal properties and must be accounted for during production and final product application design. To effectively capture its mechanical and thermal impacts, the proposed model utilizes a unique decomposition approach to the deformation gradient and applies the Coleman--Noll procedure and minimum dissipation potential principle to material modeling. The resulting model includes suitable Helmholtz free energy and dissipation potential assumptions, which allows for realistic simulations of crystalline region formation, degradation, and temperature changes through a combination of mechanical, thermal, and diffusion equations. Numerical implementation based on the finite element method provides simulation capabilities for real-world applications and validation against experimental data.

To analyze the impact of external magnetic fields on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with
meager and intermediate filling factors, we computationally investigate the
interplay between magnetism and the helical Dirac interface in Bi$_2$Se$_3$.
A London-Wolf free-energy formalism is adapted to model Bi$_2$Se$_3$ as a
vector-order parameter, accounting for the inhomogeneous distribution of
carriers within the oxide layer. We derive the London and Abrikosov-Wolf energy
equations, solving them numerically for meager and intermediate filling factors
under magnetic fields up to 20 Tesla. We also investigate the interplay
between magnetism and the helical Dirac interface, examining the possibility
of $d$-vector ordering in the Bi$_2$Se$_3$ interface.

Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to various channel disturbances, such as phase and Doppler shift. Its basic structure makes its implementation uncomplicated, involving the product of a received baseband signal and a time-reversed version of one symbol duration. Nevertheless, it experiences reduced signal-to-noise ratio compared to coherent detection methods. In this research, the performance of conventional differential detection is enhanced through increased delay periods. By doing so, the minimum required signal-to-noise ratio at the symbol level is shown to decrease by 3 dB for various CPM types. Additionally, we demonstrate that the minimum required signal-to-noise ratio can be achieved under quasi-static fading conditions, with rates less than 1 bit per symbol and tight delay constraints. Our study further includes simulation results for real CPM types under Rayleigh fading.

A previously reported finding from the research of the 1990s and 2000s, indicating that the square root of the ratio of the variance to the mean of quantum energy density adds up to 1.395, has been confirmed through numerical calculations using quantum chromodynamics. This confirmation was achieved by analyzing data from five different lattice configurations in thermal environments. The same result has been obtained using different types of quantum systems, including non-abelian gauge theories and fermionic systems. The same thermodynamic quantity that measures the relative fluctuations of energy density in these systems has also been given a quantum name, and its relationship with the expectation value of energy density was established using a mathematical formula. This research has further supported the concept that the same general principles apply to the behavior of quantum systems and classical ones.

Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured as conditional relationships (if X, then Y), stands out from existing datasets that categorize object-based knowledge.  Our analysis reveals that relationships between events, entities, and locations account for the majority of everyday inferences, while most connections are made between events and events, and entities and entities.  With over 1,500 predefined categories of situations covered by the atlas, ATOMIC demonstrates a broad scope of applicability in assessing the performance of intelligent machines in understanding everyday inferences.  Our assessment metric, based on precise semantic matching, enables seamless integration of the atlas into existing evaluation frameworks.  The comprehensive nature of ATOMIC, validated through comprehensive surveys with 500 participants, positions it as a definitive benchmark for assessing the commonsense reasoning capabilities of artificial intelligence systems in real-world applications.

This research develops a novel framework for executing portfolio optimization tasks using QuMonte Carlo methods on a Quantum Computer, based on Constrained Stochastic Dynamic Programming. By leveraging the QuickSelect operation, our algorithm achieves a significant reduction in quantization error while minimizing the required number of samples. We demonstrate that our algorithmic approach exceeds the benefits of applying the HHL Quantum Algorithm, yielding an estimated 50-fold improvement in processing power when executing portfolio optimization for a hypothetical asset portfolio on a realistic Quantum Processor Simulator. Furthermore, our results indicate that our algorithmic solution can handle portfolio optimization for multiple assets with up to 20 assets within the simulation capabilities of current Quantum Processors. When executing a more complex portfolio optimization task that incorporates credit risk analysis for a company with 5 divisions, our algorithmic solution shows the potential to provide a 1000-fold increase in processing power over classical methods once near-term Quantum Computers are further developed.

To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models using multi-modal training, we must overcome two significant hurdles: synchronizing the speeds of video and text data, and aligning the temporal structure of feature sequences. In this study, we introduce a novel attention mechanism, the Temporal Alignment Module (TAM), designed to align the temporal structure of input sequences, and incorporate a feature extraction module to handle speed differences and data efficiency. We further propose a multi-modal training method, combining self-supervised learning with a contrastive loss function to reduce semantic differences between modalities. Our proposed method, TAM-CTC, demonstrates superior performance in multi-modal training for both pre-trained and from-scratch models, with significant improvements in ASR accuracy: our best model achieves a 9.8% absolute improvement in word error rate (WER) compared to the baseline, and surpasses a strong baseline CTC model by 13.6% WER when trained from scratch.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. Under the total variation distance, we require $k_n$ to grow at a rate no faster than $n/(\log n)$. For the coupling distance, we can choose $k_n$ to be any sublinear function of $n$. We also prove as well as an associated convergence in law result for the associated order statistics. These results can be obtained under the additional assumption that the variance of $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $n$. We develop our main distance-independence theorem by utilizing coupling with random permutations of the first $k_n$ elements, which can be either ascending or descending. We demonstrate that the asymptotic behavior of the minimum of $\pi_n(i)$ for $1 \le i \le k_n$ is achievable through a combination of an independent identity and the results of Kolmogorov. We also show that our asymptotic results for the minimum or the order statistics $\pi_n(k_n)$ hold under the condition that the variance of $k_n$ is sublinear. We

Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly NbN nanowires, indicate the presence of a critical voltage threshold for dc conduction below which coherent quantum phase slips dominate, potentially blocking conduction. The critical voltage of these nanowires is observed to be tunable using an adjacent gate electrode and varies significantly in response to applied voltage, aligning with expected results of quantum interference but exhibiting unanticipated periodic variations. The magnitude of these periodic variations far exceeds predictions based on capacitance alone and presents a discrepancy in understanding this phenomenon, especially after observing sudden period shifts during measurements. The possibility of attributing the behavior to granular Josephson junctions within the nanowires is also considered, offering an alternative explanation for the findings.

Our proposed approach tackles the challenge of forecasting video footage that is shot from a completely new angle, based on previously captured images of the same scene. Unlike conventional methods, our network is capable of predicting videos shot from angles as extreme as 45 degrees, without being limited by the field of view. Through rigorous testing on two extensive datasets, our research shows that our model can accurately forecast videos shot from novel viewpoints, even at very large angles. Our proposed network also achieves notable performance enhancements in comparison to rival techniques, surpassing them by a significant margin in viewing angle. Our model's effectiveness is further supported by in-depth analysis, revealing that it excels particularly in forecasting short-term future views and in scenarios with minimal occlusions.

In this research, inter-orbital coupling was demonstrated using femtosecond laser writing, which enables orthogonal modes in a photonic lattice to couple with each other at different spatial frequencies. We designed an asymmetric double-well structure to create a spatial reservoir where mode-beating occurs due to identical sites being out of phase, allowing for a narrow frequency range to couple with the desired mode. The degree of coupling was tested under varying beam waist sizes and orientation, resulting in controllable coupling coefficients ranging from 2.1 to 63.7 kHz, which can be used for multiplexing, mode-rotation, and coherent population oscillations in a parametric quantum circuit.

The Ω-baryon, which contains sss quarks and has only been marginally detected in past experiments, has primarily been studied using theoretical methods so far. A study aims to explore this particle's properties utilizing a quark model with linear confining forces. Calculated resonance masses are presented for the ground and excited states of S, P, D, and F quark systems. A linear nature of the Regge trajectory, supported by calculated data and magnetic moments, has also been examined. This study compares its results to other approaches and available experimental evidence.

Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods. To better understand and quantify the transport and dispersal of aerosols carrying viruses in these settings, we developed a comprehensive mathematical model. This model accounts for the movement of inhaled air, the formation and settling of aerosol droplets, and the variation in ventilation methods. We have also created a numerical method to solve this problem, using a multiscale model that combines high-resolution modeling in a local area around the head and neck, with results from a larger bus model. To validate our approach, we compared the results from our model with data from experiments measuring aerosol dispersion on a bus. These comparisons show that our model effectively captures the same patterns of aerosol distribution and settling, even with different ventilation methods.

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves a rise in Spin-Orbit Coupling near a strong spin-orbit material's interface with an adjacent layer. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, such as graphene and ferromagnetic layers, and controlling Spin-Orbit Coupling may lead to the discovery of novel phases in superconductor and semimetallic systems. In the study presented here, magnetoelectrical transport and anomalous Hall resistance measurements reveal increased Spin-Orbit Coupling at a EuS interface with a two-dimensional ferromagnetic layer, sustained over several micrometers and influenced by a magnetic field to demonstrate the separation of Spin-Orbit Coupling from magnetization. Notably, the Spin-Orbit Coupling can be manipulated through the application of a magnetic field and interface disorder, offering a means of controlling this effect and exploring its impact on non-equilibrium electronic dynamics.

This paper provides approximate solutions to the fractional time-independent Schrödinger equation in $N$-dimensional space for a generalised Mie-type potential, expressed as $V(r^{\alpha})=A/r^{2\alpha} + B/r^{\alpha} + C$, with the fractional parameter $\alpha$ affecting the space variable $r$. As $\alpha$ equals 1, this potential reduces to the original Mie-type potential, commonly studied in physics. Using the Jumarie type fractional derivative approach, solutions are obtained and expressed in terms of the Mittag-Leffler function and a fractionally defined confluent hypergeometric function. Verification of results is achieved by comparison with existing works, particularly for $\alpha=1$. Numerical examples, including a diatomic molecule, demonstrate energy eigenvalue and bound state eigenfunction calculations.

Neural networks exhibiting high levels of performance often suffer from being non-
linear and non-Euclidean in their function representations. As a result, they are
difficult to train due to becoming stuck in local minima. In an attempt to
overcome this challenge, an approach called Deep Linear Neural Networks (DLNNs)
has been proposed. This model, composed of linear layers only, has demonstrated
the ability to achieve high performance levels after undergoing significant
deformations. In response, the task of intentionally deforming existing neural
networks to achieve a linear representation has been framed as a new optimization
problem. This problem-solving process is further complicated by the introduction
of an external constraint that requires the network to maintain low levels of
Lipschitz continuity. This condition essentially prevents the network from being
permitted to distinguish between the training data and data unrelated to it. In
response to this challenge, a novel algorithm known as DLI-Net has been created
which leverages the use of an external network to train a linear network that
meet the requirements of meeting the non-maturity criterion with data that is
unrelated and to train the original network with data that is similar to the
training data. This algorithm has been successfully tested and resulted in a
linear network that accurately predicts the features of data that is unrelated and
also efficiently applies to various types of data.

We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan dilepton and same-sign same-flavour (SSSF) production in LHC runs 2 and 3. Our analysis reveals that SSSF processes can provide important insights, offering sensitivity to a specific type of exotic particle known as vector leptoquarks that affect tau leptons. Furthermore, we develop a strategy for combining Drell-Yan and SSSF production data, finding that combining these processes can significantly enhance the vector leptoquark exclusion limit by up to a factor of twenty for type-B R-parity violating SUSY.

Due to rising radiation exposure levels, there is a growing interest in estimating individual radiation doses from whole-body positron emission tomography (PET) scans. In order to determine the radiation dose from PET scans for individual patients, a new approach has been developed that combines image processing, Monte Carlo simulations, and machine learning tools. Initially, the method was tested using standard PET scans of phantoms and then applied to actual scans of 30 patients. The average dose calculated for the head, heart, lungs, liver, kidneys, and the remainder of the body compared to reference values showed variations of up to threefold in certain organs for some patients, indicating a need for organ-specific dose estimation. Furthermore, the analysis demonstrated that the water equivalent diameter factor overestimates the actual dose, particularly for smaller patients. A nonlinear regression model was developed to predict the dose for individual patients and organs, which could be beneficial for adjusting organ-specific doses based on patient body weight.

A linguistic analysis known as centering theory (CT) explains how coherence in conversations emerges from the connections between successive statements. This paper explores the link between CT and advanced computer systems that identify relationships within a text. By developing specific metrics and a search algorithm, the study between CT-based expectations and actual connections in a text can be measured. The evaluation was conducted using two types of texts: a randomly selected subset of the BankWire corpus and written narratives collected from university students. The results show that measurements of relationships within the texts can be accurately predicted by both CT and a different model before being compared to the actual connections found in the texts. The difference between predicted and actual connections can be used to measure the coherence of the texts. This measure aligns with other metrics used to evaluate the coherence of texts. The method introduced in this research can be applied to evaluate coherence based on other expectations about text structure.

Recently, WiFi has become a prevalent technology for positioning methods within indoor settings by utilizing fingerprinting techniques. In this context, our study focuses on determining how various transformations impact collected data and how they affect positioning results. A representative method, DRENSHL, is utilized to analyze the effects on positioning outcomes when real measured data is used with previously created fingerprints. Our experimental findings reveal that both signal strength and timestamp are affected by movements, ambient temperature, and time of day. Consequently, positioning results experience significant errors. Nevertheless, utilizing DRENSHL leads to a significant improvement in positioning results when considering both signal strength and timestamp in real-time measurements in combination with previously created fingerprints.

The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically restricts the maximum beam current that can be achieved through a high-power gun or a photo injector. A research innovation presents a solution by introducing a novel septum cavity to alter the longitudinal to transverse phase space, thus impeding the beam breakup mode and allowing for higher beam currents to be achieved with a photo injector. Calculations demonstrate that a specially designed septum cavity can thwart the beam breakup instability at the Canadian Light Source III, enabling the use of a gun that produces higher beam currents with the photo injector, and similarly allows for a larger dynamic range with the Linac at the Next Generation Light Source.

To extend the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy, the one-loop CEV for two gluons with low rapidity ordering must be known. In this work, the dispersive part of a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory was calculated under a NMRK kinematic limit and used to determine the one-loop CEV for two gluons within the same kinematic constraints. The calculated CEV matches the predicted form of the Belskii-Dita-Frankel equation and confirms previous findings about the one-loop CEV for two gluons in a MRK kinematic limit. Additionally, the relationship between the CEVs for two gluons and the six-gluon amplitude in a BFKL kinatic limit was confirmed. The associated calculations were performed using the six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory under a NMRK kinematic limit.

Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights into the behavior of surface-grafted polymers in various scenarios, including the use of curved substrates with pressurized gaps, vesicles, and toroidal surfaces. However, these models have a critical limitation, as they assume that the free end regions of the brush are devoid of polymers, which is not applicable when curved surfaces with narrow gaps are used. In this study, we introduce a new method of analyzing elongated brush behavior on the surface of a sphere, incorporating regions far from the sphere's equator where the pressure becomes too great and the polymer chain exclusion is not significant. We found that our model can reproduce the scaling properties observed in the non-exclusion zone area and provides the necessary pressure and curvature data to predict suitable surface curvatures. Our research demonstrates that the scaling behavior of elongated brushes can vary greatly, depending on the surface curvature, and we have made our model available online as an interactive tool.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph.

Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-based method enhanced the image quality compared to standard techniques, particularly in replicating complex diffuse emissions from the galactic plane. These models can simplify image analysis by sidestepping assumptions about emission patterns, yet they also struggle with temporal analysis due to their inability to account for source variability and flux drift. Nonetheless, machine learning-based pre-processing improved the signal detection threshold by 0.5%, demonstrating the potential benefits for large-scale space missions like Fermi that are tightly resource-constrained.

Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems by employing a basic model where multiple agents take sequential actions. The model stipulates that each agent's action is chosen from a finite set defined by a set of feasible options, and their goal is to maximize their individual payoff while the overall social payoff is influenced by the actions taken. We prove that using the serial dictatorship mechanism for actions taken in a predetermined order will result in action combinations leading to high social and individual payoffs. Furthermore, we demonstrate that payoffs achieved through this method can be nearly optimal, with a margin of improvement that depends on the specific problem being solved.

We designed two distinct point spread function (PSF) filtering techniques to identify wide binary asteroids within wide field surveys, specifically the Pan-STARRS1 survey, which observed the sky for near-Earth objects and asteroids. Our approach entailed comparing each data point to every other data measurement taken within a defined celestial area, with the primary goal of detecting objects in close proximity to known binary asteroids. A second method involved creating a model of each known binary asteroid and identifying observations that aligned with a particular orbital path, with the aim of detecting data points along that path. Both strategies were effective in identifying measurements that matched the characteristics of known binary asteroids and could potentially be missed by standard reprocessing algorithms. However, only a small percentage of detected measurements, approximately 0.01%, showed signs of being related to binary asteroids and required further investigation. One notable example is the discovery that the binary asteroid asteroid (769) Kempo might be part of a larger orbital chain, albeit one that is unstable over a long period, with estimated mass of 1.3 kilogram or roughly 2.9 times the mass of 769 Kempo itself.

This research supplements the findings related to the specified context, model, and estimation methods initially presented by Auerbach in 2019. The paper's first section explores the asymptotic behavior of the estimators presented in section 2 of the Auerbach's work. The second section investigates extensions to the models and methods used in section 3 of the Auerbach's paper. The third section applies the models and methods used in section 4 of the Auerbach's work to estimate peer effects within networks. The fourth section offers an asymptotic analysis of the estimators proposed in section 5 of the Auerbach's paper. The paper's final section discusses the role of identification schemes in model asymptotics.

This study introduces novel versions of the Leibniz Rule for the Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order fractional integral and derivative. It derives key formulas, including product, quotient, and chain rules for both the integral and differential operators. Specifically, four distinct product rule formulas, four quotient rule formulas derived from product rule types, and four chain rule formulas have been established.

This research focuses on a collaborative storytelling activity known as "Dungeons and Dragons" where players collaborate with a referee known as the Dungeon Master to create an engaging narrative through interactive dialogue. By analyzing the conversational dynamics, our study aims to demonstrate how the Dungeon Master's engaging storytelling techniques, encoded as actions in our proposed framework, encourage players to explore new story paths and engage in creative problem-solving with the group. Utilizing multi-agent theory and dialogue systems as a foundation, we develop a computational model to replicate the Dungeon Master's engaging storytelling actions and evaluate its effectiveness through a narrative coherence assessment and player acceptance test.

The complex relationships between protein knots, geometry, and dynamics motivate the use of topological simplifications, as seen in the study referencing the paper by Michaudell et al., which found that the majority of covalent bonds in proteins can be connected in cycles, in turn made up of linked loops, without needing to consider the geometric details of these cycles and loops. Based on this concept, the field of protein topology was created, which includes methods for comparing and analyzing these topological cycles, also known as knotoids. In the paper under consideration, a method is developed for mapping the knotoids of which proteins are composed to their corresponding cycle diagrams, enabling the comparison of protein knotoids based on their topological properties rather than geometry. Furthermore, the authors created an online database called the Protein Knotoid Atlas, which features real-world knotoids extracted from the protein data bank PDB, in addition to conducting an in-depth analysis of 245 PDB entries, including the identification of 78 distinct knotoids, analysis of knotoid occurrence patterns, and comparison with existing theoretical models.

Let $\omega$ be a Kaehler form on the real $4$-dimensional torus $T^4$. Given that it fulfills an irrationality criterion which can be realized via an arbitrarily minor adjustment, the one-point blowup $X$ of $(T^4, \omega)$ possesses a well-defined symplectic mapping class group associated with it, denoted as $\pi_0\mathfrak{Symp}^{01}(X, \omega)$. We prove that this group is isomorphic to the mapping class group of the surface obtained by blowing up $T^4$ at one point, which is equivalent to the braid group $B_4$. This distinctive characteristic stands out due to its contrast with the lack of a clear description of the standard symplectic mapping class group of $X$. The proof of this distinctive characteristic relies on an analysis of the symplectic mapping class group of the one-point blowup of $T^4$ following an approach that was initially employed by Gambaudo and Giroux to determine the mapping class group of the one-point blowup of the complex projective plane $(\mathbb{CP}^2, \omega_{FS})$ under the condition that a specific integer is not an algebraic number.

A detailed investigation of the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem has been conducted with an emphasis on its underlying mathematical structures drawn from Lie algebras, geometry, and number theory. The principles of NG theorem were examined in relation to spontaneous symmetry breaking (SSSB), revealing its implications for the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. In essence, the anomalous NG theorem was found to indicate a deviation from linear behavior in the long-wavelength limit, thereby violating the assumption of the standard NG theorem that leads to the NG mode being decoupled from other physical fields. As a result, the long-wavelength NG mode becomes strongly coupled with other physical fields in the process of SSB, resulting in the loss of its independent identity. Consequently, these couplings give rise to the distortion of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, transforming it into the Schrödinger uncertainty relation. The research into the anomalous NG theorem was motivated by the Higgs mechanism in the Standard Model and the phenomenon of SSB symmetry breaking in general. The study's framework can be applied to any theoretical model featuring the NG mechanism and SSB symmetry breaking, offering new insights into the relationship between the anomalous NG theorem, the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, and the Schrödinger uncertainty relation.

Recent studies indicate that enhancing models with counterfactual data can improve resilience and help prevent model drift.  Nevertheless, producing a vast quantity of high-quality counterfactual data, as required for scaling counterfactual learning, is difficult due to the extensive need for human input.  Our novel framework, dubbed DISCO, addresses this challenge by automatically generating a large quantity of counterfactual data without human intervention.  It leverages a generator that produces imperfect data, which is subsequently corrected by a small group of trusted instances through a voting-based method.  Our framework extends this process on a large scale by utilizing an external pool of unlabelled instances.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by conducting multiple experiments under different settings and scenarios, achieving notable improvements over current methods of generating counterfactuals, particularly in classification tasks where complex datasets and language models are involved.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the growth of high-quality, lattice-mismatched materials at reduced temperatures with minimal material waste. Despite its potential, the actual mechanism behind remote epitaxy remains unclear due to inadequate data. Our study demonstrates that precise control over growth conditions can result in the heusler compound TaGdSb3 collapsing into a highly ordered overlayer on graphene at the graphene edge, demonstrating edge-specific heusler epitaxy. By varying the growth position, we found that TaGdSb3 can also grow homogeneously on graphene with a well-defined crystal structure, presenting the first evidence for true remote epitaxy. Our findings open up a new paradigm for heusler compounds, and our approach shows that the strict requirements for direct heusler epitaxy can be bypassed, allowing for the growth of a wide range of heusler compounds on graphene with remote epitaxy.

A code is referred to as $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear if it results from a particular type of encoding process called the Gray image of a code that has properties derived from $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-additive code, given a prime number p greater than two. This paper specifically delves into the examination of the rank and dimension of the kernel of these $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes. Furthermore, specific limits on the rank of $\Z_3 \Z_9$-linear codes and the dimension of the kernel of $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes have been established and detailed examples are provided.

Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes.  However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required, a problem that limits the availability of such datasets in real-world applications.  This paper explores an uncharted territory in this area, investigating the potential benefits of singular positive labels in a dataset like ImageNet, a substantial dataset with extensive multi-class classification capabilities.  A novel technique known as ``one-shot pseudo-conditioning'' was developed to assign pseudo-conditions for each data sample utilizing recurrent neural networks.  This technique is simple to apply to existing large datasets with single-class annotations following a straightforward procedure.  The results obtained from utilizing this technique to assign conditions to ImageNet data demonstrates the potential applications and the necessity for further research in this area.  The code required to replicate this research has been made accessible online.

The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and associated physical states. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as a kind of inverse procedure for state representation through an abstract adjoint relationship, capturing fundamental aspects of the algebra's underlying properties. This abstract adjoint relationship must be seen within the context of weakly natural transformations, a concept that arises from categorifying functors. This formulation of the relationship provides the basis for interpreting the inherent mathematical structure in physical terms.

The cause behind gamma-rays in nearby galaxies emitting high energy radiation remains unclear.  Hadronic radiation from the disk around supermassive black holes at their centers may provide a possible explanation, yet it requires significant accretion.  A new possibility is presented where magnetic fields near the black hole suck in and trap relativistic particles that can produce gamma-rays through electric currents in jets.  This approach is applicable to all galaxies with active black holes and can produce gamma-rays in a specific energy range but requires certain conditions to do so.  A recent detection of gamma-rays in the nearby galaxy M87 by the Fermi Space Telescope suggests that gamma-ray radiation may be widespread in the local universe with the help of its magnetic fields.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are effective for this purpose.  However, accurate condition identification from auscultation recordings is complicated due to the diverse sounds and noises present.  This study presents a novel method, the Condition-Aware Spectral Representation Network (CASRN), designed to automatically analyze cardiac sounds and assign a spectral representation that reflects the underlying pathology.  CASRN consists of three key components: a feature extraction module, a condition-aware encoder, and a spatial transformer, all working together to produce a distinct spectral representation for each condition.  The network's effectiveness is evaluated on the PhysioNet Challenge 2019 dataset, with results showing that it surpasses current state-of-the-art approaches in classification and feature extraction tasks.  Furthermore, CASRN successfully generates condition-specific spectral representations that align with medical expertise.

The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. However, a major difficulty in using these devices arises from data aggregation platforms not being tailored to individual users' needs. Another significant challenge arises from user data not being personalized due to large amounts of aggregated data from multiple users. This research introduces FDRec, a recommendation system designed to address both issues. FDRec takes into consideration user features such as activity levels, sleep patterns and sports history and uses a deep neural network to predict user interests and preferences. Furthermore, the system is scalable to handle large amounts of user data. Experimental results show that FDRec achieves better performance compared to other recommendation algorithms like NCF and DRMM under various evaluation metrics.

This study classifies portfolio optimization strategies with higher order moments including skewness and kurtosis to aid Hedge Fund practitioners in navigating various paradigms and methodologies. Key research approaches, such as utility theory and multi-objective optimization, are reviewed, with an examination of their benefits and limitations.

In large-scale organizations, recruiting involves interviewing a substantial number of applicants, a time-consuming and intricate process. To achieve efficiency, a well-planned approach is crucial. This task involves selecting applicants, scheduling interviews, and choosing panel members for each interview, all while adhering to various constraints. Due to the complexity and vast number of possibilities, accurately assessing all possible plans becomes impractical, making an optimal plan hard to guarantee in the general sense. However, for recruitment processes, often common strategies like round-robin or random matching can provide acceptable solutions. In this paper, we focus on one such approach commonly employed in the public sector, where multiple panels assess candidates, and our goal is to plan interviews so that each panel consists of exactly the same candidates, in a different order. We frame this as an instance of the sliding window problem, and our contribution includes presenting a dynamic programming algorithm that yields optimal solutions for small-scale problems, as well as a more efficient greedy algorithm that solves larger-scale problems. We also test these algorithms against real-world data.

This study tackles a complex control issue, where the costs of transitioning between states can change suddenly in time. Our main achievement is to derive several important properties of the cheapest control policy in this dynamic context. Notably, we demonstrate that at any given moment, either the optimal strategy will remain stuck in a particular state or quickly switch between two states with a specific, well-defined structure. Additionally, we can determine when the optimal approach will stay in one of these double-state cycles and, in cases where there are multiple such cycles, determine which one is the most beneficial to follow. Our proof of these results involves establishing the properties of a related stochastic process, as well as developing an efficient numerical method to approximate the optimal control policy through simulation.

To explore the significance of new physics, our research investigates asymmetric leptoquark pair creation in the Large Hadron Collider to provide solid constraints on its properties and aid in identifying its potential. Asymmetric production stands out from conventional methods as leptoquarks created in proton-proton collisions aren't opposite charges. To make this process possible, we outline the required conditions and list all relevant combinations of leptoquark groups that can create it. Furthermore, our studies in the Standard Model and its scalar extensions demonstrate how to integrate this process into reinterpretations of existing experiments, producing more accurate leptoquark property constraints.

We analyzed a sample of 106 galaxies with both submillimeter and radio data, and examined the relationship between gas temperature and luminosity in different nuclear regions. Our analysis in nuclear regions found that gas temperatures deviate from linearity with respect to stellar mass, black hole mass, and bolometric luminosity. We also found that the assumption of nonthermal radio continuum as a mass indicator for nuclear regions is valid, with some variation depending on galaxy type. We then compared the temperatures in bulge and disk components and found that temperatures in bulge components are higher than those in disk components, with a mean temperature ratio of 1.24. We also found that the assumption of a linear relationship between gas temperature and luminosity in disk components is generally valid, with some variation depending on luminosity. We then used a radiative cooling curve to estimate the density of thermal electrons in galaxies and found that the assumption of a linear relationship is not valid for bulge components, with densities ranging from 10 to 100 times higher than typical ISM densities. We also examined the nonthermal radio continuum as a mass indicator for nuclear regions and found that it breaks down at high luminosities, with a transition mass of 103.5, and that the assumption of a linear relationship is not valid for low masses, with a mass threshold of 1.2x10^8. Levenshtein initially introduced the sequence reconstruction problem in 2001.
It deals with a scenario where a transmitted sequence is altered by either a channel
with at most $r$ errors or one-way communication channels, and the goal is to determine
the shortest sequence of channels that can restore the original sequence.
We demonstrate that it's possible to recreate the original sequence using repeated
transmissions of the distorted sequence to certain channels, assuming there are $c$
available channels, and we show these solutions are optimal under specific conditions.
A key finding shows that transmitting a sequence to specific channels, which can
be chosen from a set of $c$ available channels with up to $d$ errors, is sufficient
to recover the original sequence if the number of required transmissions is less
than the minimum cycle time and if the sequence and channels meet particular
divisibility criteria. Additionally, we provide a constructive approach to solve
the sequence reconstruction problem for a wide range of parameters, including cases
where the number of available channels equals or exceeds the number of errors.

Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable 
of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual supermassive black hole binaries, 
which are likely the most feasible sources for PTA at their most sensitive levels. 
For the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna and PTA, we have developed a code 
called PTAfast4BH to efficiently calculate PTA signals from these binaries at 
different stages of their evolution. Our approach outperforms existing methods in 
the same time frame by 10,000 times and 100 times for quasi-circular and general 
orbital configurations respectively, allowing for the calculation of signals for 
millions of binaries within the mass range $10^5-10^{10.5} M_{\odot}$ in a matter 
of seconds. We have further optimized our program to leverage multi-core CPUs 
efficiency, enabling the computation to be parallelized across numerous processors. 
By employing a cut-off frequency similar to LISA, we are able to sidestep the 
complication of waveform evolution during merger and ringdown phases, focusing 
instead on the precursor oscillations that dominate PTA signals. We have created 
databases containing pre-coalescence waveforms for approximately 1.5 million binary 
systems based on different mass ratios, from nearly parabolic to nearly polar-orbit 
configurations, and we have made these resources publicly available for the PTA 
community.

We investigate a one-dimensional system of ASEP with periodic boundary conditions, focusing on the dynamics of a second-class particle and its surrounding sea of bulk particles. By analyzing the asymptotic behavior of the system over an infinite time period, we find that the second-class particle converges to a constant velocity, represented by the negative of its initial position relative to the system's size. Additionally, we derive a formula representing the sea of bulk particles as a stationary coherency packet with sharp edges, formed through the combination of wave packets that rapidly dissipate over time. Our results are supported by both analytical Jacobian calculations and numerical density profile simulations.

This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic, focusing on the fundamental aspects of the models mentioned in the paper that was published on February 20, 2020, by the National Academy of Sciences. The paper discusses the classic characteristics of the Kermack-McKendrick models, critiques their limitations, and explores the diverse methods that have been employed to generalize and refine the models over time.

Our research focuses on an ultracold system of spin-zero atoms located in an optical lattice, where we can observe interactions, a tool known as photoassociation, and a phenomenon called spin-exchange collisions influencing the formation of atom-molecule pairs. By manipulating these interactions and a small energy difference, we can create long-lived atom-molecule bonds, known as Feshbach molecules, within the optical lattice. However, this process is complex and depends on various factors, such as the strength of spin-exchange collisions and whether they result in loss of atoms, and whether a tiny energy difference exists, which can either prevent or allow the formation of molecules. In our experiments, we investigated multiple interactions and resonances with a beam of light, creating atom-molecule pairs under different conditions, and ultimately forming magnetic molecules within an optical lattice, with durations of up to 30 milliseconds before they dissolved into atoms.

Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that creates links between stored data and encoded information stored in DNA. Unlike previous approaches, this architecture allows for easy data updates and management, in addition to facilitating the incorporation of additional metadata into stored data. In our design, each piece of stored data is associated with a unique barcode, and we've developed methods for efficiently locating and modifying specific pieces of stored data. Our results show that with a 10-base encoding method, a single oligonucleotide tube can store approximately 1.3 terabytes of data on DNA, and we successfully retrieved and updated specific pieces of data from as few as 100 to 100,000 pieces currently stored in DNA.

This study deplores the reliance on solvers that minimize errors through iterative computations for predicting river flow velocities and flows. In contrast, it suggests leveraging machine learning algorithms that quickly deliver precise solutions. An analytical expression is derived to predict water depth in rivers, and it is subsequently used to train various models, including decision trees, support vector machines, and neural networks. The performance of these models is assessed in relation to the accuracy of their predictions for different flow rates and velocities. The research reveals that efficient machine learning algorithms capable of handling complex problems and large datasets, such as neural networks and residual, can accurately predict water depth and flow velocities with high precision. Furthermore, using these models yields precise solutions for the Saint-Venant equations with minimal computational effort. The research demonstrates a practical application of these models in a scenario where water is being released from a dam, finding that they can efficiently solve the problem with a significant reduction in computational time. The research also highlights the necessity of ensuring data quality to ensure model effectiveness.

HDR photography combines multiple photos captured at various exposure levels
to counterbalance digital cameras' limited dynamic range. This research presents a
technique for automatically determining optimal exposure settings for smartphone
images by utilizing the camera's inherent characteristics. Furthermore, an innovative
image fusion method is introduced, leveraging optimization and weighted averages.
These techniques are applied to a mobile HDR application, demonstrating the
feasibility of the approach. Comparative assessments are also conducted to
demonstrate the introduced solution's efficiency in comparison to established methods.

The proliferation of machine learning models that consume additional information
for predictions and inference has given rise to causal deep learning. This field
investigates neural networks with side information to achieve accurate and
inference-enabled predictions. While it has achieved significant progress, the
research gap remains substantial, with many open questions awaiting solution.
This survey seeks to delve into the underlying theory and delve into the
practical applications of the causal deep learning technique known as neural
archival learning (NAL). From a theoretical standpoint, it delves into the
underlying theory of NAL, discussing its connections to regression, estimation
of causal effects, and multi-task learning. From a practical perspective, it
examines NAL in two contexts: (1) using side information to achieve precise
predictions, and (2) utilizing external knowledge for inference. It also delves
into the challenges, potential research directions, and the possibilities
available within the NAL framework.

This note presents a new category of map-structured mappings, known as oriented colored broken submersions, which the b-principle governs. This category includes, as subcases, oriented colored submersions, submersions with specific index properties, Lefschetz maps, proper maps, and smooth locally flat maps. Each of these specific cases has its own associated invariant - the Euler characteristic of the domain being non-negative, the Euler characteristic of the domain being equal to the Euler characteristic of the domain pre-image, the Lefschetz number being 1, the map being proper, and the map being locally flat, respectively. A map from a given space to a standard target space is considered a solution to a problem defined by the conditions mentioned above. The aim of the b-principle is to assert that any problem defined by these conditions has a solution, with the solution being a map that is oriented colored broken submersions, as long as the space in question has a certain Euler characteristic and does not contain certain topological components.

This research compares the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve the large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the performance of the methods, including the use of multiple subdomains, different grid types, various heart muscle mesh sizes, and the presence of electromechanical force fields. The study reveals that the BDDC method generally outperforms the AMG solver, with the greatest difference observed when solving the small subproblem equations using the algebraic solver. Additionally, an in-depth examination is performed to highlight the performance characteristics that influence the scalability of the methods.

Standard diffusion models can fail, particularly when influenced by correlations and variations, where mean squared displacements grow in a linear manner with time. We investigate the spread of a fractional Brownian population exhibiting time-dependent and diverse diffusion characteristics. Our primary objective is to establish the relationship between these individual characteristics and the population's spatial distribution as observed over time. We examine the applicability and limitations of this approach to a broad category of self-similar diffusion processes, utilizing a general framework that is subsequently applied to recognized processes such as Laplace diffusion, nonlinear diffusion, and their variants.

A fundamental theory is developed to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between the modes of dielectric optical resonators, with the scope being applied to both passive components and photonics circuits. This theory, presented in a mode basis, allows for the calculation of outgoing light modes resulting from the interaction between an input light mode and the resonator. It is demonstrated that linear interactions can lead to mode scattering, coupling can result in the conversion of modes, and in the presence of nonlinear interactions, a specific scattering process converts two frequency-symmetric modes into a sum and difference of frequencies, effectively behaving as a parametric amplifier. This theory is then applied to a nonlinear cavity with a specific geometry, the Kerr beam splitter, and its properties are compared with an ideal beam splitter. It is also possible to implement this theory using a classical discrete time dynamics approach, which can be realized using a white light interferometer as a classical analogue system. It is found that this analogue system can exhibit the same properties as the nonlinar cavity, specifically amplifying the difference frequency and suppressing the sum frequency, with the added benefit of being a large parameter system.
